title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compares two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for end‑to‑end correctness, with preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate shared per pair). Execution: 120 paired tasks (planned episodes 240, completed episodes 240), one shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was shared, the confirmatory test measures validator‑acceptance parity of identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness; preregistered hypotheses about independent generator/repair superiority (H1,H2) are therefore unobserved in this execution. We present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), an explicit evidence‑to‑claim table, a nearest‑work comparison matrix, and minimal preregistered design changes required to discriminate architectures in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes matters for operational NetOps: constrained translation plus formal verification aims for strong device guarantees, while agentic LLM pipelines promise flexibility and on‑the‑fly repair. We preregistered the head‑to‑head question: for intent‑driven changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (reachability and policy isolation): (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 froze a paired estimand (A − B) over N = 120 paired intent tasks balanced by vendor×topology and specified analysis by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Crucially, the preregistered execution semantics used shared_initial_candidate: each pair received one identical LLM candidate (a single model call shared between arms). That semantic intentionally removes generator variance and therefore makes the run a measurement of downstream deterministic validator acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than a direct comparison of independent generator/repair robustness. The present paper reports the fully archived artifactized execution, the exact numeric outcomes, an evidence‑to‑claim mapping requested by peer review, a nearest‑work comparison matrix, and precise minimal preregistered protocol modifications needed to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.
sections.related_work: Two literature streams set context. (1) Formal translation→verification approaches constrain configuration outputs and apply deterministic checks to guarantee device‑level properties; classical network verification and intent synthesis work (e.g., "Don't Mind the Gap" and SymNet) established the value of formal checking for correctness and scalability [10,11,12]. (2) Recent LLM‑based NetOps and agentic AIOps work demonstrates flexible generation, repairs, and the need for deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [13,14,15]. Prior empirical studies vary in whether they evaluate independent generation variance, repair coverage, or validator acceptance and typically do not combine preregistration, paired designs, and fully archived deterministic validation. Our run is a narrowly scoped, artifact‑backed instance that clarifies what a shared_candidate paired execution reveals (validator acceptance parity) and what it, by design, cannot resolve (generator/repair superiority). Representative verified prior works used for comparison appear in the nearest‑work matrix and reference list below [10,11,13,16].
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed: (i) target estimand = paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B); (ii) N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks balanced across 3 vendors × 3 topology classes (distribution specified in preregistration); (iii) generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one shared model call per pair); (iv) model declared = gpt‑5‑mini; (v) validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (vi) adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; (vii) allowed repair iterations = 1 (applied only if repair loop triggered). The preregistration included a power rationale targeted at detecting a ≈15pp paired difference with 80% power under independent generation variance; that calculation assumes independent sampling and therefore does not apply under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Preregistered analysis methods: paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Execution semantics and accounting. Execution followed the preregistration and the execution manifest records: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Relevant archived artifacts include execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha prefix c5b16909), execution/model_configuration.json (sha prefix 1acce925) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (sha prefix 9f25790c). Task generation and difficulty calibration. Tasks were drawn from a deterministic synthetic NetOps task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that produced intents, initial states, required sequences, and canonical reference answers; representative tasks and per‑task manifests are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha prefix 8f1a570a). Constraints and scoring. The validator applied full_intent_constraint_validation rules (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0); per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) include normalization, validation_before/after metadata, and repair_applied flags. Repair policy. The system recorded repair_applied = false for every episode (no repairs executed); this is evident in the scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) and in analysis/missingness_summary.csv (sha prefix be8cd717).

Marginal success rates: baseline (translation‑first) = 120/120 = 100.0%; guarded (agentic) = 120/120 = 100.0%. Primary estimand: paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric results and the bootstrap parameters are archived in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Repair outcomes and secondary estimands. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (no repair loops executed); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage and mean repair iterations are therefore unobserved in this execution and provide no evidence to compare repair efficacy between architectures. Representative per‑task example. Pair pair‑000001 artifacts (execution/responses/task‑000001‑shared‑initial.txt and execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) show the shared_initial_candidate content and validator normalization; the validator trace records validation_before.valid = true, validation_after.valid = true, and repair_applied = false. Deterministic reconciliation. The reconciler confirms episode/accounting consistency: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 120, baseline_success_count = 120, guarded_success_count = 120 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation and what the execution measures. Because the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the collected data measure validator‑acceptance parity of identical candidates delivered to two downstream orchestration paths; they do not measure independent generation variance, repair coverage differences, or an architecture’s ability to generate correct candidates when operating independently. The degenerate contingency (all pairs concordant success) produces a pinned bootstrap CI and McNemar p = 1.0; these statistics correctly reflect the observed data but do not inform H1/H2 about independent generator/repair superiority. Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (compact table). The table below maps each preregistered hypothesis/estimand to the measurement actually performed, the artifact(s) supporting the reported outcome, and a verdict.Provisioned evidence‑to‑claim table (inline):

Evidence‑to‑Claim Table:
1) H1 (Paired difference A − B > 0 for end‑to‑end correctness): tested? NO — measured estimand = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate (not independent generation). Supporting artifacts: preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 (preregistration_sha256 reported in execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini; sha prefix 1acce925), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0; sha prefix 9f25790c). Verdict: untestable for independent generation given shared generation semantic.
2) H2 (Agentic pipeline achieves higher repair coverage): tested? NO — repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes. Supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied=false per episode; representative file execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json), analysis/missingness_summary.csv (sha prefix be8cd717). Verdict: unobserved in this execution.
3) Primary estimand executed: validator‑acceptance parity (A and B acceptance status for identical candidates). Supporting artifacts: analysis/condition_summary.csv (baseline 120/120, guarded 120/120; sha prefix 9c77c96f) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv. Verdict: tested — result = parity (0.00 difference).

Nearest‑work comparison matrix (compact). We position the present run relative to representative verified prior work (columns indicate whether each study experimentally exercised independent generation variance, repair loops, validator acceptance, emulator/hardware):
• INTA (Y. Wei et al., ICNP 2025, 10.1109/icnp65844.2025.11192391): focuses on intent translation with LLM agents—covers independent generation in reported experiments; limited deterministic validator focus. Present run: covers validator acceptance (yes), independent generation (no), repair loops (no), emulator (yes, Mininet‑derived). 
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026, 10.23919/ifipnetworking70592.2026.11578993): presented a self‑correcting multi‑agent pipeline for Kubernetes network policy (includes repair/verification loops). Present run: repair loops unobserved; differs in shared_candidate semantics.
• Weighted NetKAT / verification literature [10,11]: strong emphasis on formal verification and translation→verify architectures; experimental emphasis on verifier guarantees and what‑if analyses rather than LLM generation. Present run aligns with verification emphasis but isolates validator acceptance with shared candidates.

Operational implications and recommended minimal protocol modifications. The present artifact bundle documents a reproducible protocol for measuring validator regression and acceptance parity when generation is held constant; this is useful for validator testing and for checking deterministic verifier behavior across orchestration wrappers. To discriminate architectures on independent generator/repair performance the preregistration must be modified (all changes are preregistered options and will appear in future manifests): (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm requests an independent LLM generation per pair (model_calls_used would rise to 240 for initial candidates alone, matching the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 240), (ii) permit multiple sampled generations per arm (expose generator variance and increase model_calls accordingly), (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 can be observed and compared, (iv) increase device fidelity (use hardware or higher‑fidelity emulation) to reduce simulator‑to‑device contamination risk. Each modification has direct, manifestable consequences (higher model_calls_used, nonzero repair_applied counts, additional provider_call events) and therefore can be validated in the archive.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifactized paired comparison of translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines across 120 intent task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both pipelines accepted the identical LLM candidates for all tasks, yielding 100% success in each arm (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), paired difference 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs occurred (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); consequently preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage/iterations are unobserved. The run therefore documents validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent architectural robustness. We provide a compact evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a nearest‑work comparison matrix, representative per‑task validator traces, and precise minimal preregistered changes that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in future artifactized runs.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
